displayQuote: If you can't explain something to a first-year student, then you haven't really understood it

meta.title: Who really said "If you can't explain something to a first-year student, then you haven't really understood it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Feynman never said it in these words. It paraphrases David Goodstein’s account: ‘I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.’
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you can't explain something to a first-year student, then you haven't really understood it'?
meta.ogDescription: The documented line is Goodstein’s account of Feynman on spin-statistics — and Feynman said ‘we don’t really understand it,’ not ‘you haven’t.’

answer.label: Not Feynman’s wording — a paraphrase of a real remark
answer.sourceLine: Feynman is not recorded saying or writing this sentence anywhere. What is documented is a conversation recalled by his Caltech colleague David L. Goodstein: asked to explain why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics, Feynman said “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it,” then came back a few days later with “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.” The thought is genuinely his — the tidy rule is someone else’s summary, and it quietly flips his point, because Feynman said we (physicists) don’t understand it, not you haven’t.

source.heading: What Feynman actually said, and where

docMeta.dd: Feynman’s Lost Lecture: The Motion of Planets Around the Sun
David L. Goodstein, in the reminiscence chapter (‘Feynman: A Reminiscence’), p. 52 — W. W. Norton, 1996; the same anecdote is cited by Wikiquote to Goodstein’s Physics Today article of February 1989
Paraphrase — found in no Feynman text

source.excerpt: Feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I said to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.”
trail: The words Feynman is actually documented as saying come from David Goodstein’s reminiscence in Feynman’s Lost Lecture, and Caltech’s own Engineering & Science reprinted the passage in 1996 ↗: “I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.” The subject was one specific physics problem — why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics — not a study technique.

Wikiquote carries the anecdote only in its ‘Quotations about Feynman’ section ↗, cited to David L. Goodstein, “Richard P. Feynman, Teacher,” Physics Today, volume 42, number 2, February 1989, pp. 70–75, at p. 75. The sentence people quote today appears nowhere on that page.

Wikiquote’s talk page files the popular wording under ‘Unsourced’ ↗, notes that it “Seems a paraphrase of the exchange,” records the variant “If you can’t explain it to a six year old, you don’t really understand it,” observes that it is “Sometimes attributed to Einstein,” and pins the book passage to Chapter 2, p. 52.

The 1996 W. W. Norton edition is catalogued and scanned at the Internet Archive ↗. Searching the full text of the book returns the exchange exactly as quoted above and returns the popular sentence not once.
source.excerptNote: The narration is Goodstein’s; only the words inside quotation marks are Feynman’s, as Goodstein recalled them. The 1996 book and Caltech’s reprint of it both read “we don’t really understand it”; Wikiquote’s citation of the 1989 Physics Today telling reads “we really don’t understand it.” Neither is the sentence in circulation.

author.name: Richard Feynman
author.heading: About Richard Feynman
author.metaLine: 1918–1988 · American theoretical physicist · Nobel laureate in Physics, 1965
author.bio: Richard Feynman shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on quantum electrodynamics, devised the diagrams that carry his name, and taught at Caltech from 1952 until his death in 1988. His two-year introductory course of 1961–1964 became The Feynman Lectures on Physics, and that reputation for making hard physics plain is exactly why aphorisms about explaining things simply get pinned on him. He became a public figure again in 1986 on the commission investigating the Challenger disaster.

Feynman, Teacher,” Physics Today 42, no. 2 (February 1989): 70–75, at 75. The sentence “If you can’t explain something to a first-year student, then you haven’t really understood it” appears in neither, and in no work by Feynman; it is a later paraphrase.

misattribution.heading: A real remark, sanded into a slogan
misattribution.intro: Feynman is one of the internet’s biggest quotation magnets, and this is the most instructive kind of case: not an invention out of thin air, but a genuine remark reshaped into a maxim that says something he did not say.

items.why: It appears in no Feynman book, lecture, letter or interview. What exists is David Goodstein’s recollection, published the year after Feynman’s 1988 death; Wikiquote lists the circulating sentence as unsourced and notes it “Seems a paraphrase of the exchange” ↗.

Feynman’s point was that physics collectively had no beginner-level account of why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics — “That means we don’t really understand it” ↗. The slogan converts a confession about the state of the field into a test of the individual reader.

items.scope: The same idea under another name
items.why: The cousin line ‘if you can’t explain it simply, you don’t understand it well enough’ is pinned on Einstein just as often. Its nearest attested root is the ‘explain it to a barmaid’ maxim, which Quote Investigator traces to Ernest Rutherford, earliest citation 1955 ↗ — an article that never mentions Feynman at all.

Goodreads’ community entry credits the line to The Science Book: Big Ideas Simply Explained ↗ — a present-day reference book repeating the saying, not a Feynman source. Goodreads itself notes its quotes are community-added and unverified.

misattribution.truthLine: Feynman really did make the point — once, about one hard problem, in Goodstein’s telling: “I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it” ↗. The neat sentence people quote is somebody else’s summary of that.

context.heading: Why the real version is better
lead: The remark grew out of a specific frustration. Goodstein — who by his own account joined the Caltech faculty in the period just after Feynman’s 1965 Nobel Prize — asked him why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics. It is a result that is easy to state, provable at a high level, and stubbornly resistant to an elementary explanation. Feynman took it on as a teaching problem, and lost.

That is what makes the paraphrase a downgrade. Feynman was not handing anyone a self-help test; he was conceding that a piece of physics he could calculate with fluently was a piece of physics nobody could yet make plain. ‘We’ meant physicists. The slogan says ‘you.’
detailsBody: Goodstein told the story more than once. Wikiquote cites it to his article “Richard P. Feynman, Teacher” in Physics Today for February 1989, the year after Feynman’s death, and it appears again in the reminiscence chapter of Feynman’s Lost Lecture (1996) — the book he and Judith R. Goodstein built around a guest lecture Feynman gave to the Caltech freshman class in March 1964.

The tellings differ by a word: the 1996 book and Caltech’s reprint of it read “we don’t really understand it,” while Wikiquote’s citation of the 1989 Physics Today version reads “we really don’t understand it.” That small wobble is itself the point: the wording of a remembered remark is not fixed, which is exactly why a polished, quotable version of it should be treated as a paraphrase rather than a quotation.
context.pull: ‘We don’t really understand it’ — not ‘you haven’t.’
